original_question: Show that gamma_1, the imaginary part of the first nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function, is irrational.
target_in_paper: The draft targets Section "Theoretical problems," Problem #2 (Alexandre Bailleul): "Show that γ1 is irrational," which the paper explicitly presents as "a concrete instance of the above problem" from Problem #1. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
correct_elements: Your draft is already extremely close to the paper’s official formulation. It correctly singles out γ1 and asks for its irrationality, and it correctly identifies γ1 as the imaginary part of the first nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function. This is essentially the paper’s Problem #2 with only minor stand-alone clarifications missing. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
missing_details: To match the paper’s notation exactly, γ1 should be specified as the smallest positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of ζ(s); the notation section records γ1 ≈ 14.135. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
For full stand-alone precision, "irrational" should be made explicit as meaning γ1 ∉ ℚ. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))

Because zeros come in conjugate pairs, the positivity of the ordinate is an implicit detail worth stating explicitly when defining γ1. This is supplied by the nearby definition of an ordinate as a positive imaginary part. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
The problem is unconditional: although RH, GRH, SZ, and LI are defined nearby, Problem #2 is not stated under any of those hypotheses. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))

The paper-faithful scope is the specific constant γ1, not the broader neighboring problems of proving that ζ(s) has at least one irrational ordinate or that all positive ordinates are not all rational multiples of one another. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
refined_question: Let γ1 ≈ 14.135 denote the smallest positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s). Prove that γ1 is irrational; equivalently, prove that γ1 ∉ ℚ. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
justification: The nearest official statement is exactly Problem #2 in the paper, not the broader Problem #1. The nearby context needed to make the question self-contained is minimal but important: the notation section defines γ1, and the opening lines of the theoretical-problems section explain that an ordinate is a positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of an L-function. Therefore the sharp, paper-faithful rewrite is the unconditional irrationality of the first positive ordinate γ1 of ζ(s), with no extra hypotheses and no broadening to other ordinates or other L-functions. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03530))
